extracted.intended_audience: newsroom journalists, editors, and other newsroom staff (e.g., Washington Post staff; editorial teams managing online corrections)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures for issuing, placing, approving, and wording online corrections, clarifications, and editor's notes for news content (stories, blogs, galleries, video). Covers workflow, approval, placement, and wording conventions to ensure transparency and consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and transparency: revise the story and append a correction
rubrics_metrics.description: We are committed to accuracy and transparency. We generally revise the story to make it accurate AND append a correction to the file. Typically, online corrections read like this: “Correction: An earlier version of this story incorrectly reported …”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not leave the mistake within the text of the story while also adding a correction; both fixing the text and adding a correction go hand in hand. Use explicit wording that states what was wrong so readers understand the correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not unpublish without senior-editor approval; replace removed content with an editor's note
rubrics_metrics.description: We should never 'unpublish' stories from the Web. Once a story is up, however, the content can be removed with the approval of a senior editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If content is removed, it must be replaced with an editor’s note explaining the reason for the deletion (example: “Editors’ Note: This article was published inadvertently and has been removed.”). Try to avoid unpublishing whenever possible; if you must remove content, publish an explanation/apology at the same URL and be explicit about why the article was removed (avoid vague phrasing like 'published inadvertently').

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor involvement and approval for substantive errors
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor must be involved in cases of substantive errors. Reporters should not ask producers to correct stories. An online correction can be approved by either a section assignment editor or an editor on the Universal Desk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed is important; if the assignment editor is not immediately available, e-mail the Universal desk (universal@washpost.com) and copy the assignment editor. Clarify (internally) what qualifies as a 'substantive' error — plagiarism and fabrication are assumed, but guidance is needed for errors that may undermine a story's central thesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrections submission workflow and syncing with print
rubrics_metrics.description: The page for submitting corrections has fields for the URL of the story and the text of the online correction. Your online correction should already be up by the time you file a correction for the print edition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When copy editors sign off on a print correction, they will check the online correction and change it if the two are not in sync. This workflow is intended to ensure consistency between print and online corrections; follow the submission form fields and timing expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of corrections should reflect the gravity of the error
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement for corrections reflects gravity of error. A serious error must be noted at the top of the story, blog or graphic. For smaller errors, corrections can be appended at the bottom as a footnote, and noted next to the error in the text of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be consistent across stories to avoid reader and staff confusion; picking one standard and sticking with it is recommended. For blogs, the tone of the correction can sometimes match the blog and a strike-through is an acceptable alternative. For galleries, photo caption corrections should be placed underneath the photo’s caption; if a photo is removed, the correction should appear in the gallery blurb. Corrections can be posted directly into a video blurb.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifications should be rare and require top-editor approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarifications should be rare and must be approved by the editor-in-chief, or managing editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The memo provides no clear distinction between a correction and a clarification (or between an editor’s note and a clarification). For clarity, prefer a simpler taxonomy (e.g., corrections and editor's notes) and strictly limit the use of 'clarification' to avoid multiple overlapping forms that create confusion and poor execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: State clearly what was wrong (no prohibition on repeating the error)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no policy against 'repeating the error.' We generally do say exactly what was wrong, to make it absolutely clear what is being corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit in wording so readers can see precisely what was incorrect; transparency is prioritized over avoiding repetition of the original mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed of online corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: In an effort to ensure that errors online are corrected as quickly as possible, corrections should be posted promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed matters; use the approved approval/escalation path (assignment editor or Universal Desk) if immediate sign-off is needed. Aim to have the online correction up by the time a print correction is filed.
